e1.title: Spear-phishing link harvests a ClearPay credential
e1.how: The attacker sends a spear-phishing email with a link to a cloned Microsoft 365 login page spoofing ClearPay’s IT helpdesk domain. The victim enters live credentials, captured in real time by the phishing kit. No attachment or malware, so email-gateway attachment scanning never triggers.
e1.leverage: Those credentials are the only thing standing between the attacker and ClearPay’s key vault. Because the vault enforces no second factor, one harvested password is enough to reach and export a live vendor API key in the next hop.
e1.determined: This edge sits at the very start of the chain. It carries no dollar figure itself — no Meridian system is touched yet — but its control_multiplier of 1.0 records that nothing stopped it, which feeds the end-to-end path bypass the engine multiplies later.

e2.title: Static vendor API key replays into Meridian
e2.how: The stolen credential opens ClearPay’s key-management portal (again, no MFA) and exports a live API key scoped to Meridian’s vendor integration gateway. The key authenticates cleanly — it is a valid machine identity with no IP allow-list, so the request is indistinguishable from normal vendor traffic.
e2.leverage: A long-lived static key means the attacker inherits a trusted machine identity without ever touching a Meridian employee account. There is no login anomaly to page on, because from Meridian’s side this is the vendor doing exactly what the vendor always does.

refs.lbl: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts — Defense Evasion / Persistence

e2.determined: The key’s granted scope — read from the IAM export, not the vendor’s stated need — is what sets the eventual blast radius. Bypass probability 1.0: a static key with no MFA is a control that is effectively absent.

e3.title: Over-scoped gateway reaches the HR file-share
e3.how: The API key authenticates to the Vendor Integration Gateway. Its scope was provisioned broadly at onboarding for "partner integration" and never narrowed to the read-only invoice endpoints ClearPay actually uses — so it also carries write access to the HR file-share.
e3.leverage: The attacker uses the unneeded write scope to pivot off the vendor integration and into an internal system, turning a partner API into an internal foothold. This is the over-provisioning that converts a vendor incident into a Meridian incident.
e3.determined: This is the first hop the graph scores as a privilege boundary crossing. The engine reads the scope directly from config; the gap between what the key can reach and what it was meant to reach is exactly what "over-provisioned" means.

e4.title: Cached federated token discovered
e4.how: Pivoting through the write-scoped HR file-share, the attacker finds a cached OAuth session token left in a config file by a legitimate service account — never rotated or deleted after a prior migration.
e4.leverage: The cached token still carries active federation trust to Meridian’s identity provider. Rather than crack anything, the attacker simply reuses valid authentication material to move toward the IdP — a credential-hygiene failure, not an exploit.

refs.lbl: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

e4.determined: The engine scores this as a distinct control-bypass factor — the leftover token — separate from the IAM scope issue on the previous hop, so the two failures are not double-counted.

e5.title: Session minted as Treasury-Approve
e5.how: The cached token’s federation trust lets the attacker mint a full session at the IdP. That session inherits the legacy "Treasury-Approve" group — a role grouping created for a since-dissolved team and never cleaned up in the 2024 reorg.
e5.leverage: Privilege escalation happens without a single failed-login alert: the attacker never guesses a password, they inherit an over-broad role that already exists. The session now holds payment authority it was never meant to have.

refs.lbl: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts — Privilege Escalation (TA0004)

e5.determined: This hop sets the financial ceiling. The engine looks up every role the session inherits and takes the highest transaction authority among them — Treasury-Approve is what turns a data-access incident into a payments incident.

e6.title: payment_write on the legacy Treasury-Approve role
e6.how: With Treasury-Approve privileges the session authenticates directly to the Core Payment System. No further exploitation is needed — to payments-core this is a valid, trusted login carrying a $2.4M / 24-hour transaction ceiling.
e6.leverage: The attacker stages transfers to match the metadata of a routine weekly ClearPay settlement batch, keeping them below manual-review thresholds. SIEM coverage on this vendor→treasury path is 0%, so the transfers accrue with nothing to page the SOC.
e6.determined: This is the hop that locks in the number: exposed_capacity_24h $2.4M (read from the gateway config) × detection_window_factor 1.0 (0% path coverage) × control_multiplier 1.0 = $2,400,000. A configured limit, not a probability estimate.

phases.detail: A phished ClearPay employee hands over an O365 credential, which opens the vendor key vault and exports a live API key. It replays into Meridian’s gateway — no MFA, no IP allow-list — and looks identical to normal vendor traffic.
The over-scoped gateway key carries write to the HR file-share. Pivoting through it, the attacker finds a cached federated token left in a config file after a prior migration.
The cached token mints a session in the legacy Treasury-Approve group — a role grouping never cleaned up in the 2024 reorg. No failed-login alert ever fires.
Treasury-Approve carries a $2.4M / 24-hr ceiling. Transfers are staged as routine ClearPay settlement batches; SIEM coverage on this vendor→treasury path is 0%, so nothing pages the SOC.

e1.title: Payments API key committed to a public repo
e1.how: A partner integration commits a live corporate-payments API key into a public GitHub repository. Automated secret scanners — the same ones defenders run — surface it within minutes of the push, and so does the attacker.
e1.leverage: The attacker never has to breach a perimeter: the credential is already outside it. A single balance-read call confirms the key is live and privileged, giving a trusted foothold with no login anomaly to detect.
e1.determined: This edge starts the chain with control_multiplier 1.0 — a leaked static key has no second factor to stop it. It carries no dollar figure itself; it feeds the end-to-end path bypass the engine multiplies later.

e2.title: Leaked static key authenticates to the payments API
e2.how: The key authenticates to the Corporate Payments API. It is a long-lived machine identity: no MFA is possible, and no IP allow-list constrains where it can be used from, so the request looks identical to legitimate partner traffic.
e2.leverage: By reusing a valid machine identity, the attacker acts as the partner integration itself. There is no user account to lock, no password to reset — the key is the identity, and it is already trusted.
e2.determined: The key’s granted scope — read from the IAM export, not the partner’s stated need — sets the eventual blast radius. Bypass probability 1.0: the authentication control is effectively absent.

e3.title: Enumerate accounts under the shared originator profile
e3.how: The key reads the shared ACH originator profile and lists every corporate account grouped under the same originator ID — a mapping of where funds can legitimately be pushed from this identity.
e3.leverage: Shared originator profiles let one compromised key see and act across many accounts. The attacker uses this to pick beneficiary structures that spread the fraud thin enough to stay under per-transaction review.
e3.determined: This hop widens reachability but sets no ceiling on its own. The engine records it as a discovery step that makes the origination hop’s full limit realistically usable.

e4.title: Leftover ach_originate scope on the machine identity
e4.how: The key still carries an ach_originate scope, granted for a 2025 migration and never revoked. With it, the identity submits ACH origination batches directly to the ACH gateway — no escalation needed.
e4.leverage: This is the over-provisioning that turns a read-only-looking partner key into a money-movement capability. The attacker submits origination batches the integration was never designed to touch.
e4.determined: This hop locks in the number: exposed_capacity_24h $4.1M (the ACH gateway’s configured same-day origination ceiling) × detection_window_factor 1.0 (0% path coverage) × control_multiplier 1.0 = $4,100,000. A configured limit, not a probability estimate.

e5.title: Batches staged as routine NACHA files
e5.how: Origination is split across multiple beneficiary accounts and formatted to match routine NACHA batch metadata, keeping each entry below the per-transaction review threshold.
e5.leverage: By shaping the fraud to look like normal batch activity, the attacker avoids the manual-review queue entirely. The fraud engine is tuned for card-not-present patterns, so batch ACH anomalies never trip it.

refs.lbl: Audit Log Management — the coverage gap exploited

e5.determined: A defender gap, not a new privilege: it drives the 0% detection coverage on this path, which is why detection_window_factor stays at its 1.0 ceiling rather than trimming the exposure.

edges.evidence: CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Bleed): an out-of-bounds read on the NetScaler appliance leaks a valid session token from a legitimate user, replayable without credentials or MFA.
The leaked web session cookie is replayed to reach an internal jump host in the DMZ. The session is already authenticated, so no MFA challenge is presented.
From the jump host the attacker assumes an over-privileged IAM broker role that fronts payment services — a standing role with wire-origination rights it should not hold.
The broker role can originate wires through the SWIFT connector with no second approver enforced on this corridor.
The jump host also holds a reusable token for the card-automation service account — a second, independent route off the same foothold.
The automation account can drive bulk virtual-card issuance. A velocity check trims part of the volume (path_control_multiplier 0.80) but does not stop the flow.

changes.label: Emergency NetScaler remediation: patch + invalidate sessions
changes.note: Patch CVE-2023-4966 AND terminate active/persistent sessions (per NetScaler guidance). Patching alone would not revoke the already-stolen session — invalidation is what actually closes the shared entry. Both branches fall.

changes.label: Revoke automation card-issuing scope
changes.note: Branch-level: removes bulk card issuance from the automation account. Cheap and fast, but the wire branch remains.

changes.label: Enforce SWIFT dual-approval
changes.note: Branch-level: a mandatory second approver breaks single-actor wire origination. Leaves the card branch open.

changes.label: Segment the jump host
changes.note: Network control at the shared choke point. Closes both branches, but the segmentation project is the highest-effort option and may disrupt legitimate flows.

changes.label: Evidence gap: card detection delay unknown
changes.note: Unknown ≠ safe: with no detection_delay evidence, the engine holds the card branch at its full ceiling and marks the verdict incomplete.

e1.title: Citrix Bleed session-token leak (CVE-2023-4966)
e1.how: Lion Bank’s internet-facing NetScaler ADC/Gateway is unpatched against CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Bleed). A crafted request triggers an out-of-bounds read that returns memory contents, including a valid session token belonging to a legitimate authenticated user.
e1.leverage: The attacker replays that token to inherit an already-authenticated session — no password, and critically no MFA prompt, because the session predates the second factor. A real, widely-exploited 2023 vulnerability, not a hypothetical.

refs.lbl: Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway — sensitive information disclosure (Citrix Bleed)

e1.determined: This edge starts the chain with a path_control_multiplier of 1.00 — an unpatched, exploitable appliance offers no control to reduce it. It carries no dollar figure itself; it feeds the deterministic multiplier the engine applies at each reachable financial node.

e2.title: Session replayed past MFA to the jump host
e2.how: The stolen web session cookie is replayed against internal services, landing the attacker on a DMZ jump host. Because the token represents an established, authenticated session, the identity provider never issues an MFA challenge.
e2.leverage: This is the step that converts an edge-device flaw into interior access. The jump host is the shared choke point from which both later branches originate — which is exactly why segmenting it (a remediation fix) closes both routes at once.

refs.lbl: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie

e2.determined: A distinct control-bypass factor (the replayable session) scored separately from the CVE on the previous hop, so the two failures are not double-counted. Multiplier 1.00 on this hop.

e3.title: Assume the over-privileged IAM broker role
e3.how: From the jump host the attacker assumes an IAM broker role that fronts payment services. The role is a standing grant carrying wire-origination rights far beyond what the automation workflow it was created for actually needs.
e3.leverage: No account is modified and no elevation control is defeated — the attacker simply inherits a role that is already too powerful. That is incorrect privilege assignment, and it is what makes the high-value wire branch reachable.
e3.determined: This hop opens Branch A. The engine reads the role’s granted rights from config, not from its intended use — the gap between the two is the over-privilege this scenario is built on.

e4.title: Wire origination through the SWIFT connector (Branch A)
e4.how: With the broker role, the attacker originates wires through Lion’s SWIFT connector. No second approver is enforced on this corridor, so single-actor origination succeeds and looks like normal treasury activity.
e4.leverage: Branch A is the high-value, fast-detection route: Lion’s payment-anomaly rule flags the corridor at 6h, so exposure is bounded by how much of the 24h capacity can move in that window.
e4.determined: Branch A exposure = exposed_capacity_24h $6,680,000 × detection_window_factor 0.25 (delay 6h) × control_multiplier 1.00 = $1,670,000. Enforcing dual-approval removes this edge and this $1.67M — but nothing else.

e5.title: Reuse an automation-account token (Branch B opens)
e5.how: The same jump host holds a reusable token for a card-automation service account. The attacker reuses it to reach the card-issuing service — a second route that shares the entry and the jump host but nothing downstream.
e5.leverage: Because Branch B is independent of Branch A, fixing one does not touch the other. This independence is the whole point of the scenario: single branch-level controls leave residual exposure on the other route.

refs.lbl: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

e5.determined: A lateral step that opens Branch B; it sets no ceiling itself. Multiplier 1.00 on this hop — the reduction on this branch comes at the issuance edge below.

e6.title: Uncontrolled bulk virtual-card issuance (Branch B)
e6.how: The automation account drives bulk virtual-card issuance through the card API. A velocity check trims part of the volume, but there is no hard limit on the automated business flow, so issuance continues at scale.
e6.leverage: Branch B is the slow-detection, larger-accrual route: the issuance monitor only flags at 18h. More of the 24h capacity is exposed, so despite the partial velocity control this branch carries the larger loss.

refs.lbl: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows

e6.determined: Branch B exposure = exposed_capacity_24h $5,000,000 × detection_window_factor 0.75 (delay 18h) × control_multiplier 0.80 (the velocity check) = $3,000,000. Revoking the card-issuing scope removes this edge and this $3.0M — but leaves the wire branch.

phases.detail: CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Bleed) is exploited against Lion Bank’s internet-facing NetScaler. An out-of-bounds read leaks a valid session token from a legitimate user — no credentials, no exploit payload on the host.
The leaked web session cookie is replayed to reach an internal jump host. Because the session is already authenticated, the MFA step is simply never presented.
From the jump host the attacker assumes an over-privileged IAM broker role fronting payment services — a standing role carrying wire-origination rights it should never have held.

Wire origination through the SWIFT connector, no second approver on this corridor. Lion’s payment-anomaly rule flags the corridor at 6h — a fast branch, but a high-value one ($1.67M realised before detection).

In parallel, the automation account drives bulk virtual-card issuance. A velocity check trims part of the volume but does not stop it; the issuance monitor only flags at 18h — slower detection, larger accrual ($3.0M).

Assumption: the 6h wire alert is first handled as an isolated payment-fraud event, not yet correlated with the stolen NetScaler session, so only the wire activity is stopped. At 18h the card anomaly is detected and the investigation connects both branches to the same compromised session, triggering full containment. Different detectors saw symptoms without recognising the shared root compromise — exactly the gap attack-path intelligence closes. (The monitoring gap on the automation path is an absent detector: a control deficiency, not an attacker action, so no ATT&CK technique.)
